# Optimization and Parallelization

Also called: Distributed Training, Per-Splat Backpropagation, Mask Gradient Computation

## Overview
Optimization and Parallelization refers to the family of techniques that accelerate the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and enable its application to large-scale scenes. It solves the computational bottleneck of differentiable rasterization and the memory limits of single-GPU training by parallelizing gradient computation, distributing Gaussian primitives across multiple devices, and optimizing the backward pass data flow. It is distinguished from standard optimization by explicitly addressing the $O(N \cdot P)$ complexity of per-pixel gradient accumulation and the VRAM constraints of billions of primitives through architectural changes to the training loop [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation], [7349-grendel-gs.md].

## Shared principles
The methods in this family share the following foundational mechanisms:

1.  **Differentiable Rasterization Core**: All methods rely on the differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer. The forward pass computes pixel color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})$ via depth-sorted alpha blending, and the backward pass computes gradients $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}$ with respect to Gaussian parameters $\theta$ [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
2.  **Gradient Accumulation**: Gradients are accumulated over multiple training steps or views before an optimizer update. In distributed settings, gradients or intermediate rendering states are synchronized across devices [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
3.  **Adaptive Representation**: Many optimization variants modify the Gaussian representation or its distribution to improve efficiency or fidelity, requiring corresponding adjustments to the gradient computation or data flow [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
4.  **Hardware Acceleration**: Methods leverage GPU parallelism, often using CUDA kernels, Tensor Cores (via GEMM reformulation), or half-precision arithmetic to accelerate the rasterization and gradient computation [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].

## Subtopics

### [MaskGaussian Gradient Computation](4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation.md)
A method for computing the gradient of the loss with respect to probabilistic masks $\mathcal{M}_i$ applied to 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself by explicitly accounting for the gradient contribution of the mask on both the foreground Gaussian color accumulation and the background transmittance path, solving the backpropagation problem through masked alpha-blending [4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation.md].

### [Training Pipeline](5325-training-pipeline.md)
The iterative optimization loop that initializes Gaussians and optimizes their parameters via gradient descent. It distinguishes itself by integrating dynamic Gaussian management (pruning, densification, cloning) within the training loop to adapt representation density to scene complexity [5325-training-pipeline.md].

### [Parallelization for Backpropagation](5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md)
A training optimization that replaces the standard per-pixel backward pass with a per-splat (per-Gaussian) approach. It addresses the performance bottleneck of atomic contention in the per-pixel approach by iterating over Gaussians and updating the gradients of the pixels they cover, yielding a 4–5× reduction in training time while maintaining numerical equivalence [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md].

### [Grendel-GS](7349-grendel-gs.md)
A distributed optimization framework that partitions the Gaussian primitive list across multiple GPUs to overcome single-device memory limits. Unlike single-machine streaming methods, it distributes the parameter table across a GPU cluster, enabling training on scenes with billions of primitives by leveraging inter-GPU communication [7349-grendel-gs.md].

### [3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details](9128-3d-gaussian-splatting-implementation-details.md)
Details the specific hyperparameters, data structures, and optimization schedules required to implement the standard 3DGS training pipeline. It sets itself apart by providing concrete numerical thresholds (e.g., opacity cutoffs, gradient thresholds) and software engineering choices (e.g., half-precision fetches) that enable real-time performance and convergence [9128-3d-gaussian-splatting-implementation-details.md].

## Background
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method introduced a differentiable rasterization pipeline that achieved real-time rendering speeds [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. However, training scales poorly with scene complexity due to the quadratic cost of gradient accumulation and the linear memory cost of storing Gaussian parameters. Subsequent works focused on parallelizing the backward pass to reduce training time [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation] and distributing the Gaussian list across multiple GPUs to handle large-scale scenes [7349-grendel-gs.md]. The integration of adaptive densification and pruning into the training loop became a standard practice to manage representation complexity [5325-training-pipeline.md].
